1226.title: Riding the ox home
1226.hook: sixth picture: he rides the ox home, playing the flute
1226.carry: practice turned to ease, still heading home
1226.howItsDone: Zen teachers use the sixth oxherding picture to describe a stage where practice no longer feels like a fight, and the image of the herdsman playing the flute on the ox's back also appears in Zen painting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth picture: the ox grows gentle through patient tending, until it follows without a rope. Your line: tamed.

Evening. A path through the fields. An ox walks slowly toward a village, and on its back sits a man who isn't holding the rope at all. He has a flute to his lips, playing a simple tune, the kind children sing. Sometimes he looks up at the clouds. The ox knows the way. Two pictures ago this same animal was dragging him toward the hills. In the sixth oxherding picture, there's nothing left to hold.
screen: `EVENING, A PATH THROUGH THE FIELDS.` → `NO HAND ON THE ROPE.` → `A FLUTE AND THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: First, the struggle is over. The preface says it plainly, in paraphrase: the struggle has ended, and gain and loss no longer grip him. The rope that went taut in the fourth picture has nothing left to do. What was effort has become ease. Second, the flute. He plays country songs, the preface says, the tunes of woodcutters and children. Nothing grand, nothing that needs an audience. In this teaching, practice that's gone deep doesn't look solemn. It looks relaxed, even a little playful. Third, he doesn't turn back. If someone calls to him, the preface says, he won't look back; if someone tugs at him, he won't stop. Ease isn't drifting. He's going home, and he isn't distracted from it. Fourth, home. Some Zen teachers read home as one's own original nature, the place the search set out from. He isn't traveling somewhere new; he's going back. His eyes are on the sky, because the path no longer needs watching. On an ordinary day, riding home can look like a practice you no longer have to force: a walk you take because you like it, a pause before meals that just happens. The verse ends, in paraphrase, by saying that whoever knows this melody needs no words.
screen: `THE STRUGGLE IS OVER.` · `A FLUTE, A COUNTRY SONG.` · `CALLED, HE DOESN'T TURN BACK.` · `GOING HOME, NOT SOMEWHERE NEW.` · then, large: `RIDING HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit however feels comfortable, and let the breath do what it's already doing, without steering it. If a sound arrives, let it be music; if a thought calls, you don't have to turn around. The ox knows the way, so fix nothing, and if a small smile shows up, let it stay.
Riding home. The sixth oxherding picture: the struggle over, the herdsman rides the ox home playing a flute, untroubled by gain and loss. Today's word.
Your line: practice turned to ease, still heading home. No hand on the rope, and nowhere else to be. Enjoy the ride.

1227.title: Ox forgotten
1227.hook: seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man alone at ease
1227.howItsDone: Some Zen teachers pair the seventh oxherding picture with the Buddha's parable of the raft to warn students against clinging even to their methods and to describe practice that no longer needs managing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sixth picture: the herdsman riding home on the ox, playing the flute, the struggle over. Your line: riding home.

The seventh picture has something missing. The herdsman is home, sitting outside a small thatched hut in the sun, rested, maybe half dozing. The whip and the rope lie idle, or hang on the wall. And the ox, the animal this whole series has been about, the one he searched for, tracked, glimpsed, caught, tamed and rode, is nowhere in the picture. He hasn't lost it. He's forgotten it.
screen: `HOME, OUTSIDE A THATCHED HUT.` → `WHIP AND ROPE LIE IDLE.` → `NO OX IN THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the ox was a way of speaking. The preface, in paraphrase, says the teaching is one, and the ox was only a temporary subject, something to point with. Like the moon coming out from behind the clouds, what was there all along is simply clear now. The ox was never a separate creature out in the hills. It was a picture for something the herdsman had all along. Second, a raft is for crossing. In an early sutta, the Buddha tells of a man who builds a raft to cross a river. Once across, he doesn't hoist it onto his head and carry it on, however useful it was. He leaves it at the shore. Teachings help you cross, the Buddha said; they aren't for clinging to. The seventh picture puts the raft down. Third, forgetting is not losing. When a skill becomes yours, you stop thinking about it. A practiced cook doesn't recite the recipe. A good friend doesn't keep a ledger. The ox is forgotten because there's nothing left to manage. Fourth, the man remains. The picture's full Chinese title says the ox is forgotten and the person remains. He's still there, at ease, someone who has finished a long job. Tomorrow even he drops out of the frame. Today the picture is restful: a quiet yard, a morning sun, tools hung up, nothing more to chase.
screen: `THE OX WAS A WAY OF SPEAKING.` · `A RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · `FORGETTING IS NOT LOSING.` · `THE OX GONE, THE MAN REMAINS.` · then, large: `THE OX FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Sit the way someone sits after finishing a long job, with no technique today: no counting the breath, no watching for wandering, no trying to be calm. If you catch yourself checking whether you're doing it right, set that down too. Just rest, the way the herdsman rests in the sun outside his hut.
Ox forgotten. The seventh oxherding picture: home and at ease, the herdsman no longer needs the ox, which was a way of pointing all along; the man remains. Today's word.
Your line: the ox forgotten. The raft is left at the shore, and nothing is lost. Rest well.

1228.title: Ox and self forgotten
1228.hook: eighth picture: both ox and self forgotten, an empty circle
1228.carry: let go of the seeker too
1228.howItsDone: In Zen, the eighth oxherding picture is drawn as an empty circle, and in Japanese Zen the enso, a circle brushed in one stroke, is practiced and hung in temples and homes as an expression of the mind at that moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man resting in the sun. Your line: the ox forgotten.

Turn to the eighth picture and there's nothing on it. No herdsman, no ox, no hut, no field, no rope. Just a circle drawn in ink, with empty paper inside. For seven pictures you've followed a man and an animal through grass and mud and weather. Yesterday the ox dropped out of the frame and the man stayed. Now he's gone too. It can look as if a page went missing at the printer. It didn't.
screen: `NO HERDSMAN. NO OX.` → `JUST A CIRCLE OF INK.` → `NOTHING MISSING.`

segments.voice: First, both forgotten. The Chinese title says it directly: person and ox, both forgotten. The verse, in paraphrase, lists them as they go: whip, rope, person, ox, all gone into emptiness. Yesterday he let go of what he was chasing. Today he lets go of himself as the one who chased it. Second, no place to stand. The preface says he doesn't linger where there is awakening, and passes quickly by where there is none. It isn't that he vanished. There's just no fixed spot left to point at and say, there he is, the enlightened man. Third, no praise can reach it. The preface mentions birds bringing flowers, an old story of a hermit so holy that birds brought him offerings, and says that praise would mean nothing here. The verse adds: the sky is too vast for anyone to survey; a snowflake can't fall on a blazing furnace. Even the idea of being special melts. Fourth, a circle is whole. An empty frame could look like loss, but a circle is unbroken. In Japanese Zen, drawing a circle in one brushstroke, the enso, became its own practice, showing the mind at the moment of the stroke. The emptiness here isn't a blank where something used to be. It's the paper the whole story was drawn on, still here when the herdsman and the ox are gone.
screen: `PERSON AND OX, BOTH FORGOTTEN.` · `NO PLACE LEFT TO STAND.` · `NO PRAISE CAN REACH IT.` · `A CIRCLE IS WHOLE.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: If there's paper and a pen nearby, draw a circle once, in one movement; if not, trace one slowly in the air with a finger. Don't fix it: wobbly is fine, it's yours. Then look at the inside, empty and missing nothing, and let breath and thoughts come and go inside it.
The empty circle. The eighth oxherding picture: ox and self both forgotten, a single circle with nothing inside, whole and unbroken. Today's word.
Your line: let go of the seeker too. Ox and self forgotten, nothing missing, and no one left keeping score. See you on the other side of the circle.

1229.title: Back to the source
1229.hook: ninth picture: rivers flow, flowers bloom, just as they are
1229.howItsDone: Zen teachers point to the ninth oxherding picture to show that awakening, as this series describes it, returns to ordinary life rather than leaving it, and some teachers invite students to sit or walk outdoors and simply look.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth picture: ox and self both forgotten, nothing but a circle. Your line: the empty circle.

After the empty circle, you might expect something grand: light, gold, a figure on a lotus. The ninth picture shows a river. A tree on its bank, a few flowers, water moving past rocks. No herdsman, no ox, no circle. It looks like a page from any landscape painter's sketchbook. That's the surprise. After all that searching and letting go, the picture comes back to the plain, ordinary world, seen clearly.
screen: `AFTER THE CIRCLE: A RIVER.` → `A TREE, A FEW FLOWERS.` → `THE ORDINARY WORLD, SEEN CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: First, pure from the beginning. The preface says, in paraphrase, that from the start things have been pure, with no dust on them. Nothing had to be built or added. The herdsman went through every stage only to see what was already the case. Second, so many steps to get back. The verse has a line that's almost funny, in paraphrase: so many steps to return to the root, it would have been better to be blind and deaf from the start. The journey wasn't wasted. He arrives where he always stood, like coming home from a long trip and seeing your own street as if for the first time. Third, things as they are. The verse ends with the river flowing on, quietly, and the flowers simply red. The preface adds that the water is green and the mountains blue. No symbolism. The river isn't a metaphor for time; the flowers aren't about beauty fading. A river and flowers, and that's enough. Fourth, watching without grabbing. The preface says he sits in stillness and watches things come together and come apart, without being caught by them. The empty circle didn't erase the world. It cleared away the reaching, and the world comes back, not as a problem to solve or a prize to win, but as it is. In this reading, the source isn't far away. It's a river on a Tuesday afternoon.
screen: `PURE FROM THE BEGINNING.` · `SO MANY STEPS TO GET BACK.` · `THE RIVER FLOWS, THE FLOWERS ARE RED.` · `WATCHING WITHOUT GRABBING.` · then, large: `JUST AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something living or moving: a tree outside the window, a plant on a shelf, clouds, even the light on a wall. Don't name it, admire it or turn it into a lesson; let it be green, or moving, or still. When the mind starts commenting, come back to looking.
Back to the source. The ninth oxherding picture: no herdsman, no ox, only a river and flowers, the world seen just as it is, as it was all along. Today's word.
Your line: just as it is. The river flows on, and the flowers are simply red. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1230.title: Into the market with open hands
1230.hook: tenth picture: he walks into town with open hands, bringing gifts
1230.howItsDone: The oxherding series ends with the tenth picture, which some Zen teachers use to stress that practice returns to daily life and service; in Zen communities this shows up as work practice, care for others and ordinary kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth picture: a river flowing, flowers simply red, the world seen as it was all along. Your line: just as it is.

The last picture is noisy. After a silent circle and a quiet river, the herdsman is back, walking into town. Barefoot, chest bare, smeared with dust and ash, a broad grin, and in some drawings a big belly too. He carries a gourd and a staff, and in some versions a sack over his shoulder. He's headed for the market, the wineshop, the crowd. No robe, no halo, nothing to mark him as special. Just a cheerful man among people, with his hands open.
screen: `BAREFOOT, DUSTY, GRINNING.` → `A GOURD, A STAFF, OPEN HANDS.` → `HEADED FOR THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: First, it ends in the market, not a cave. The series could have stopped at the empty circle or the peaceful river. The Chinese title says he enters the town with hands hanging down, an image of open, relaxed hands, ready to help. In this teaching, awakening that stays on the mountain isn't finished. It comes back down. Second, nobody can tell. The preface, in paraphrase, says his gate is shut and even the wise don't know him; his inner life can't be glimpsed. He doesn't seek out the footprints of the old masters or try to look like a sage. He goes to market with his gourd and comes home with his staff. Third, what he brings. The preface says he keeps company with drinkers and butchers, and they all become buddhas. The verse says he needs no secret art of the immortals, yet in front of him withered trees come into bloom. He doesn't preach or recruit. He's simply among people, and things around him come alive. Fourth, awakening as ordinary company. In some paintings he looks like Budai, the laughing monk of Chinese folk tradition with his sack of gifts. Mahayana teaching holds up the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening for the sake of others, and this picture shows that help as ordinary company: buying vegetables, sharing a drink, listening to a neighbor. The whole search comes out here, at a market stall, with open hands.

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up and relaxed, the way the herdsman walks into town. Bring to mind one person you'll likely meet today, at the store, the office or the kitchen, and without making a plan, let one small way of helping them come to mind: a door held, a question asked, five minutes of real listening. Then rest with open hands.
Into the market. The tenth oxherding picture: the herdsman returns to town with open hands, ordinary and unnoticed, and the people around him come alive. Today's word.
Your line: awakening comes back to help. Ten pictures, and the last one is a crowd, met with open hands. See you tomorrow.

1231.title: Rinzai and Soto
1231.hook: Rinzai stresses koans and breakthrough; Soto stresses just sitting; each honors the other
1231.carry: a koan or just sitting: two doors, one house
1231.howItsDone: Rinzai Zen students sit zazen and work on koans in private interviews with a teacher; Soto Zen students practice shikantaza, just sitting, often facing a wall. Both schools hold retreats, chant and do work practice, and some centers draw on both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenth picture: the herdsman walking into town with open hands, and the oxherding pictures complete. Your line: into the market.

Two people come home from a weekend at a Zen center. One says her teacher gave her a question with no logical answer, and she pressed on it every sitting until something cracked open. The other says his teacher gave him no question at all. Just sit, the teacher said. Don't wait for anything; the sitting itself is it. They compare notes and wonder if they went to the same religion. They did. They just walked into two different schools of Japanese Zen.
screen: `ONE GOT A QUESTION WITH NO ANSWER.` → `ONE WAS TOLD: JUST SIT.` → `SAME ZEN, TWO DOORS.`

segments.voice: First, Rinzai. It takes its name from the Chinese Chan master Linji, known in Japan as Rinzai. It stresses the koan, a short story or question from the old masters, like the sound of one hand, that can't be solved by thinking it through. A student works with a koan in sitting and in private meetings with the teacher, hoping for a breakthrough called kensho, seeing one's own nature. Second, Soto. It traces itself through the Chinese Caodong line and, in Japan, to the teacher Dogen. Its central practice is shikantaza, roughly nothing but sitting, or just sitting. Dogen taught that practice and awakening aren't two. You don't sit to get enlightened later; the sitting, done fully, already expresses it. Third, each has the other's tools. Rinzai students spend long hours in zazen, sitting meditation. Dogen himself wrote about koans, and Soto teachers use them. Some teachers call the difference one of emphasis, where each school leans, more than a wall between them. Fourth, two doors, one house. Some people are drawn to a question held until it gives way; some to sitting with no goal at all. Both call their way Zen, and both point at the ox, you might say, from the pictures just finished. Teachers in some lineages train in both.
screen: `RINZAI: THE KOAN AND BREAKTHROUGH.` · `SOTO: JUST SITTING.` · `EACH HAS THE OTHER'S TOOLS.` · `TWO DOORS, ONE HOUSE.` · then, large: `TWO SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: For the first half of the sit, hold one simple question lightly, without answering it: who is breathing? For the second half, let the question go and just sit, with nothing to find. At the end, name one thing each half offered you, without picking a winner.
Two schools. Rinzai, stressing the koan and sudden breakthrough; Soto, stressing just sitting, where practice is already awakening. Two emphases, one sitting tradition. Today's word.
Your line: a koan or just sitting: two doors, one house. Rinzai and Soto, and no winner to pick. Until tomorrow.

1232.title: Sesshin
1232.hook: days of intensive silent sitting in a Zen monastery or center
1232.howItsDone: Zen monasteries and many Zen centers hold sesshin, retreats of several days in which participants keep silence and follow a fixed schedule of sitting, walking meditation, chanting, work, meals and talks from the teacher.

segments.voice: This week the herdsman rode home, forgot the ox, forgot himself in an empty circle, and walked into the market. Yesterday: two schools, the koan and just sitting. Your line: two schools.

Before dawn, a wooden clapper sounds down a dark hallway. People roll up their bedding without a word and file into the meditation hall. Shoes in a row by the door, cushions in a row along the wall. Breakfast is eaten in silence, and so is lunch, and so is the walk back to the hall. Not for an hour, but for days. In Zen monasteries and in Zen centers in ordinary towns, this stretch of time has a name. Today's word: sesshin.
screen: `A CLAPPER BEFORE DAWN.` → `SILENCE AT EVERY MEAL.` → `NOT AN HOUR. DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Sesshin is Japanese, often rendered as gathering the mind, or touching the mind. Picture water spread thin across a table, drawn together into one bowl: attention usually scattered across a day, collected in one place. Second, the shape of a day. Mostly zazen, sitting, in periods marked by a bell, with slow walking between. There are chants, meals, a period of work and a talk from the teacher. Tradition fills the gaps with forms: when to bow, where to put your bowl, how to enter the hall. They aren't there to make it hard; they're there so nobody has to decide anything, and the mind has fewer places to run. Third, the silence. Participants don't talk, and some keep their eyes lowered. Some describe the first day or two as the loudest part: the silence outside lets every thought inside be heard. Both schools you met yesterday hold sesshin. A Rinzai one may lean on koan work and meetings with the teacher; a Soto one may lean on just sitting. Fourth, days let something settle. An evening sit is a single drop of water on a stone. Days of sitting give the mind time to settle in a way one short sit rarely can. Then it ends. People bow, speak their first words, and go home to traffic and email, bringing back not the silence itself but a memory of what a gathered mind is like.
screen: `GATHERING THE SCATTERED MIND.` · `SITTING, WALKING, EATING, WORKING.` · `FORMS SO NO ONE HAS TO DECIDE.` · `DAYS LET SOMETHING SETTLE.` · then, large: `SESSHIN.`

segments.voice: Picture one day of sesshin as if you were there: the clapper before dawn, your cushion in its row, breathing in silence beside people whose names you may not know. Then let the picture go, and notice that in this small sit you're doing the same thing they do. When the mind scatters, gather it back to one breath.
Sesshin. Days of silent, intensive practice in a Zen monastery or center: sitting, walking, eating and working, with the mind gathered in one place. Today's word.
Your line: gathering the mind. Scattered water, drawn together into one bowl. The week closes here.

fork.setup: it's the first full day of sesshin. the hall is silent, but your mind is louder than it has been in months. what does this mean?

fork.reveal: some who sit sesshin describe the first day or two as the loudest. the days that follow give it time to settle.

original.note: Japanese: sesshin, rendered 'gathering' or 'touching' the mind. some communities write it 摂心.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quiet weekend away.

what a scholar hears: two spellings, 接心 and 摂心, both read sesshin, often glossed as touching the mind and gathering the mind.
recall: meeting thoughts, not carried off by them

chat.says: Why would anyone spend days at a silent Zen retreat? Isn't an evening sit enough?

Because the rules are so strict that the hardship itself is the goal.

chat.meaning: Sesshin, gathering the mind: days of sitting let attention collect, and the forms leave the mind fewer places to run.
